clue.text: Extremely reprehensible landlord one who voted for Trump?

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters, so only the outside of reprehensible is used

parts.note: a publican is the landlord who runs a British pub

explanation.surface: A grumble about a dreadful landlord who happens to have backed Trump at the polls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' takes RE, the outer letters of 'reprehensible'. A PUBLICAN is the landlord of a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Trump stood for the Republican Party, so a voter for him is, typically, a supporter of that party; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Sturdy vehicle showing decay externally

indicators.note: externally means on the outside, so the decay word sits outside the vehicle word

parts.note: rot means decay
a bus is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A tough old car that still has rust on its outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Robust means strong and hardy, a direct synonym of sturdy.

clue.text: Standards concerning minister

parts.note: par is a standard or norm, so pars are standards
on can mean concerning, as in a talk on history

explanation.surface: Guidelines about a government minister's conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minister' suggests a politician, but it is the church sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A parson is a parish priest, a minister of the church.

clue.text: Attend American sanctuary to withdraw

parts.note: to attend is to be at an event
a retreat is a quiet refuge or sanctuary

explanation.surface: Going to an American refuge to get away from things.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom means to pull back or leave hastily, like an army falling back.

clue.text: Popular Chinese island

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

explanation.surface: A Chinese island that is a favourite with visitors.
explanation.definitionFit: Inch is a Scottish word for a small island, found in place names like Inchcolm.

clue.text: A tap losing pressure — reach with some difficulty

indicators.note: losing means being without, so a letter drops out of the tap word

parts.note: P is the physics abbreviation for pressure
a stretch can mean a reach, as of a river

explanation.surface: A tap with no water pressure can barely reach the sink.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means only just possible, by straining, hence with some difficulty.

clue.text: Have a wager against a Greek character

indicators.note: against here means placed next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: to have a wager is to bet

explanation.surface: Someone places a bet against a Greek, as if at a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'against' means 'next to': BET placed beside A.
explanation.definitionFit: Beta is the second letter of the Greek alphabet, a character in the sense of a written symbol.

clue.text: Rex is inside eagerly brewing tea

indicators.note: is inside places the king's letter within the mixed letters
brewing means being stirred up or concocted, so the letters of eagerly are mixed

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Rex, indoors, keenly makes a pot of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brewing' reworks EAGERLY into EARLGEY, and 'is inside' places R within it. 'Rex' looks like a man's name; it is Latin for king.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a black blend flavoured with bergamot oil, a well-known variety of tea.

clue.text: Behind everybody, nevertheless

parts.note: after can mean behind, as in following on
all means everybody

explanation.surface: Trailing behind the whole field, but still going.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase means in spite of everything, or despite what was expected: a synonym of nevertheless.

clue.text: Mandarin, endless stream, a curate translated

indicators.note: with no end, so the final letter of the stream word is dropped

parts.note: a burn is a Scottish word for a stream

indicators.note: translated means turned into another form, so the letters of a curate are rearranged

explanation.surface: A list of things: a Chinese official, a stream, and a clergyman whose words are translated.
explanation.walkthrough: BURN (Scottish for stream) loses its last letter to give BUR; 'translated' rearranges A CURATE into EAUCRAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandarin is a senior, powerful civil servant, the kind of official the word for a pen-pushing administrator covers.

clue.text: Good sense shown retaining original of Russian legal document

indicators.note: retaining means holding within, so the sense word keeps a letter inside it

parts.note: wit can mean practical good sense, as in 'have the wit to'

indicators.note: the original of a word is its first letter, here taken from Russian

explanation.surface: A sensible Russian keeps hold of an important legal paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retaining' puts R, the first letter of 'Russian', inside WIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A writ is a formal written order issued by a court, a type of legal document.

clue.text: What may be wanted after a night on the tiles destroyed her good faith

definitions.text: What may be wanted after a night on the tiles

indicators.note: destroyed means wrecked, so the letters of these words are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A wild night out wrecked her good faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' rearranges HER GOOD FAITH. 'A night on the tiles' is British slang for a night of heavy drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom names an alcoholic drink taken to ease a hangover, which a drinker wants after a big night out.

clue.text: Work hard to get a new advertising phrase

parts.note: to slog is to work hard and long

explanation.surface: An ad agency toils to come up with a fresh catchphrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A slogan is a catchy motto used in marketing, which is exactly an advertising phrase.

clue.text: More rum for visitor

definitions.meaning: rum means odd in British slang, so more rum is odder
a newcomer or person not from the place, someone unfamiliar

explanation.surface: A guest is given an extra helping of rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rum' is British slang for odd or peculiar, not the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of strange means odder; as a noun it means someone unknown, a newcomer or visitor.

clue.text: Public brawl — nobody's charged

definitions.meaning: a chaotic fight in which anyone joins in
no one has to pay, everything is without cost to all

explanation.surface: A fight breaks out in public, yet no one is arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charged' reads as accused by police but means asked to pay.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a disorderly fight anyone joins, and read literally says no cost to anybody.

clue.text: King, or fine British author

parts.note: George is the name of six British kings
well can mean fine, as in 'I'm well'

explanation.surface: A choice between a monarch and a fine British writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The pen name of Eric Blair, the British novelist who wrote Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four.

clue.text: Model intoxicated? Take no action

parts.note: to sit is to pose as a model for an artist
tight is informal for drunk

explanation.surface: Is the model drunk? Best do nothing about it.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom means to stay put and wait rather than act, which is to take no action.

clue.text: Naval doctor describing head of terrifying fish

indicators.note: describing here means drawing a line round, so the doctor word encircles a letter

parts.note: a surgeon is a doctor, and the title is used for a doctor in the navy

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here from terrifying

explanation.surface: A navy medic recounts a frightening fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' in its sense of drawing round puts T, the first letter of 'terrifying', inside SURGEON.
explanation.definitionFit: The sturgeon is a large bony fish whose roe is caviar.

clue.text: Computer place in centre, neat if in need of refreshment

indicators.note: something in need of refreshment is to be refreshed or redone, so these letters are remade in a new order

explanation.surface: A spot in the town centre, tidy enough if you need a drink and snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in need of refreshment' reworks CENTRE NEAT IF; it also hints at the coffee such a place serves.
explanation.definitionFit: A cafe offering computers with web access for customers is a place to use a computer while out.

clue.text: Some worship a god at temple

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some people worship a god at a temple.
explanation.definitionFit: A pagoda is a tiered tower used as a Buddhist or Hindu temple in Asia.

clue.text: Screen student in cast

indicators.note: in places the student letter within the throwing word

parts.note: to shy is to throw, so shied means cast
L is for learner, a student driver's plate

explanation.surface: A screen shows a student in a theatre cast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' looks like a troupe of actors but is the past tense of throw: SHIED.
explanation.definitionFit: To shield is to protect by covering, which is a sense of screen as a verb.

clue.text: Herb that may be found in most of NE Spanish region

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter

parts.note: Tarragona is a province and city in Catalonia, north-east Spain

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a herb grows across much of a north-eastern Spanish area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' drops the final A from TARRAGONA, a Catalan province.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarragon is an aromatic culinary herb, used notably in French cooking and in béarnaise sauce.

clue.text: Refuse to accommodate husband's party

indicators.note: to accommodate is to take in, so the rubbish word holds a letter inside it

parts.note: refuse as a noun is rubbish, or trash

explanation.surface: Someone declines to make room for her husband's party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as the verb but is the noun, rubbish. A thrash is British slang for a lively party.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrash is informal British slang for a wild, lively party or celebration.

clue.text: Leaders in Dallas Invitational set course record

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their first letters, taken here from the four following words

explanation.surface: Top players at a Dallas golf tournament set a course record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'record' looks like a best score but is a gramophone record.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc is a vinyl record, the flat round object that carries recorded music.

clue.text: Facts involving large valley

indicators.note: involving here means enfolding, so the facts word wraps round a letter

parts.note: gen is British slang for information or facts
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: The facts about a broad valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' puts L inside GEN, British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: A glen is a narrow valley, especially in Scotland or Ireland.

clue.text: Mate in capital hugging daughter in top spot, perhaps

indicators.note: hugging means wrapping round, so the phrase for a friend in the city encloses a letter

parts.note: a mate or friend is a pal
Rome is the capital of Italy

explanation.surface: A friend in a capital city with their daughter, at the best location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top spot' looks like a winning position, but it reads the same backwards letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Top spot reads identically forwards and backwards, so it is an example of a word sequence with that property; 'perhaps' marks the example.

clue.text: Combat vehicle's brown and khaki, primarily

parts.note: tan is a light brown colour

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so only the opening letter of khaki is taken

explanation.surface: An army vehicle is painted in brown and khaki camouflage.
explanation.definitionFit: A tank is an armoured tracked vehicle with a gun, built for fighting in battle.

clue.text: British want to protect the old scoundrel

parts.note: want as a noun means a shortage, or lack
to protect is to guard

explanation.surface: Britain wants to safeguard the old rascal.
explanation.definitionFit: Blackguard is a dated word for a villain or rogue, hence 'old' in the definition.
